say.text: Two patients, both blocked for 18 hours, both vomiting and in pain.
Patient A has the block high in the small bowel. Patient B has it in the colon.
Which feature set fits patient B?

choices.label: Early constipation, marked distension, late vomiting
Early vomiting, minimal distension, late constipation
Early vomiting, marked distension, late constipation

say.text: Think about how much bowel lies beyond the block. A block with little bowel beyond it behaves differently from one with a long stretch below it.
Yes. In a colon block there is little bowel beyond the block, so the constipation comes early.
Marked distension and late vomiting go with a low or colon block.
Tempting: that is the high small bowel picture, and it is right for patient A, not for the colon.
Wrong model: that one timeline holds at every level. Early vomiting belongs to a high block, so it is late in a colon block.
What is right: a colon block gives early constipation, marked distension and late vomiting.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the level again: the high pattern is right for patient A, not for patient B.

say.text: Tempting: each feature sounds right alone. Early vomiting is a real high-block sign, and marked distension a real low-block sign.
Wrong model: that features can be mixed one at a time. Each level gives its own set.
What is right: a colon block gives early constipation, marked distension and late vomiting, as one set.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-derive from the level: early vomiting and marked distension do not come together in one block.

say.text: Mechanism now. Why is absolute constipation early after a colon block but late after a small bowel block?

choices.label: Distal bowel empties first; a colon block leaves little beyond it
Colon contents are more solid, so the bowel below cannot pass
Vomiting clears the colon in a small bowel block at once

say.text: Yes. Bowel beyond the block empties first. After a small bowel block the colon still has contents to lose, so constipation is late.
After a colon block there is almost nothing distal to empty, so constipation is early. Above the block the bowel dilates with gas and fluid whatever the level.
Tempting: solid faeces look as if they would jam the bowel, so texture seems the obvious cause.
Wrong model: that the texture of the contents sets the timing. What sets it is how much bowel lies beyond the block.
What is right: the distal bowel empties first, so the length below the block decides when constipation comes.
Tempting: vomiting and constipation both empty the gut, so they seem linked.
Wrong model: that vomiting empties the colon. What empties the colon is the distal bowel emptying first.
What is right: after a small bowel block the colon empties first, so absolute constipation is late.
In mechanical obstruction, peristalsis is working hard against a fixed block.
What should the bowel sounds be on auscultation?
Ask whether the gut is still trying to push past the block. A bowel that is straining against something is not a quiet bowel.
Yes. Peristalsis works against the block, so the sounds are hyperactive and tinkling.
A silent belly belongs to the other mechanism, where peristalsis itself has failed.
Tempting: a blocked tube should be still, and a silent belly looks like a dead gut.
Wrong model: that blocked means silent. In mechanical obstruction peristalsis keeps working, so the sounds are hyperactive.
What is right: a silent abdomen means peristalsis has failed, which is adynamic, not a fixed block.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember: a working bowel against a block is noisy, not silent.

say.text: Tempting: a quiet, sluggish gut sounds like an obstructed gut that has stopped working.
Wrong model: that a block lowers the sounds. Hypoactive or absent sounds point to failed peristalsis, not to a working gut against a block.
What is right: a working bowel against a block is hyperactive and tinkling.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the direction: a block makes the sounds louder, not quieter.

say.text: Day 3 after a laparotomy, on opioids. Distension and vomiting, and the abdomen is silent on auscultation.
Most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: Paralytic ileus, from the surgery and opioids
Adhesive small bowel obstruction, from the surgery
Closed-loop obstruction of a twisted segment

say.text: Yes. After surgery, with opioids and low potassium, the gut can stop moving with no physical block.
A silent belly is the sign of failed peristalsis, so this is adynamic, not mechanical.
Tempting: adhesions are the classic post-operative cause, and a distended belly with vomiting fits.
Wrong model: that a silent belly means a mechanical block. A mechanical block keeps peristalsis working, so the sounds are hyperactive.
What is right: a silent belly after surgery and opioids points to paralytic ileus.
Tempting: a closed loop distends fast, so a large, quiet belly looks like a dramatic block.
Wrong model: that a silent belly means a closed loop. A closed loop is mechanical, blocked at both ends, and its sounds are hyperactive.
What is right: no fixed block and silent bowel point to adynamic ileus.
Known adhesive obstruction, day 1. The pain was colicky, and it is now constant and severe.
Pulse 120, one tender, guarded loop. Which reading is best?

choices.label: Simple obstruction, so continue conservative care
Obstruction resolving, so the pain is settling

say.text: Look at the word constant, then at the pulse and the tender loop. Do the three point the same way?
Yes. Constant severe pain with tachycardia and localised tenderness suggests strangulation.
Pressure first shuts venous return, then arterial inflow, so the loop turns ischaemic and gangrenous.
Tempting: the history is classic colicky small bowel obstruction, and the diagnosis is already settled.
Wrong model: that colic defines the whole course. Pain that becomes constant and severe suggests strangulation, and tachycardia adds to it.
What is right: a change from colic to constant pain, with a tender loop, needs urgent surgical review.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the pain: constant severe pain is the warning, and colic was the earlier phase.

say.text: Tempting: pain that eases can feel like the bowel is clearing.
Wrong model: that less pain means recovery. Constant severe pain is the warning sign, not a sign of decompression.
What is right: constant pain with tachycardia and localised tenderness suggests strangulation.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look at the word constant before the word settling.

say.text: Which finding suggests strangulation, rather than simple obstruction?

choices.label: Constant severe pain with tachycardia and guarding
Colicky central pain with a normal pulse
Pain that comes in waves, with a soft abdomen
Colicky pain that eases once flatus passes

say.text: Yes. Constant severe pain, tachycardia and guarding are the strangulation picture.
Raised lactate and leucocytosis, when checked, support it.
Tempting: colic is the classic first symptom of small bowel obstruction.
Wrong model: that colic and simple obstruction are the same thing. Colic is the usual start; strangulation is suggested by pain that is constant, not colicky.
What is right: colicky pain with a normal pulse and no tenderness fits simple obstruction.
Tempting: a soft abdomen is reassuring, and waves of pain sound simple.
Wrong model: that a soft belly rules strangulation out. Pain pattern, pulse and localised signs carry the weight.
What is right: waves of colic favour simple obstruction, but constant pain changes the picture.
Tempting: passing flatus means the bowel is still moving, which feels like a good sign.
Wrong model: that relief of colic shows the bowel is safe. Strangulation is recognised by constant pain, not by flatus.
What is right: colicky pain is the usual simple pattern, and constant pain is the strangulation warning.
High block: vomit early, belly flat. Low block: belly swells, vomit late.
Constant pain, tachycardia and a tender loop mean strangulation, and it needs urgent surgical review.
